newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada current account seen swinging to surplus.
newsitem.headline: Canada current account seen swinging to surplus.

text.p: Canada is expected to report its first quarterly current account surplus in 12 years on Friday, marking a major turnaround in the country's reliance on foreign capital, economists said.
Longer-term, analysts said the improvement in Canada's balance of payments will strengthen the currency and make it easier to keep Canadian interest rates low.
"What it really means is we will be less dependent on inflows of foreign capital in the years ahead," said Doug Porter, senior economist at Nesbitt Burns Inc.
The current account is a measure of a country's balance of payments with the rest of the world on trade in goods and services including investment income.
Canada is expected to report a current account surplus of C$500 million for the second quarter on Friday, according to a Reuters survey of economists.
The surplus would compare with current account deficit of C$1.94 billion in the first quarter and would mark the first surplus in Canada since the fall of 1984.

Canada has historically run a current account deficit because of its heavy reliance on foreign borrowing. About 40 percent of government debt is held by foreigners and interest payments on that debt are the main cause of the current account deficits.

"Interest payments have been flowing out of Canada quite significantly. This is one of the main things that has been pressuring the current account," said Harvinder Kalirai, Canadian analyst with New York-based financial analysis firm I.D.E.A.
In 1993 Canada's current account deficit surged to almost C$29 billion, or about 4.1 percent of gross domestic product, which was the worst performance among G-7 nations.
Two factors are responsible for the sharp turnaround in Canada's balance of payments, economists said.

Firstly, Canada's merchandise trade surplus has widened in recent years. Last year, the merchandise trade surplus rose to C$28.4 billion and is it is expected to climb even higher this year, economists at Bank of Nova Scotia said.

At the same time, Canadian governments have sharply reduced their borrowing needs. Seven of Canada's 10 provinces are expected to balance their budgets this year, and the federal government is expected to lower its deficit to C$24.3 billion in 1996/97.
Increased trade surpluses and lower foreign borrowing means Canada is now likely to begin reporting current account surpluses on a regular basis, economists said.
Over the longer term, analysts said this should strengthen the currency, narrow Canada-U.S. bond yield spreads and give the Bank of Canada latitude to keep interest rates low.

"In the past, Canadian interest rates had to be kept relatively high to entice foreign capital inflows," said Kalirai. "With Canada not needing these capital inflows anymore, Canadian interest rates don't have to be kept that high."

A narrowing current account deficit has already made it possible for the Bank of Canada to lower short-term interest rates to well below U.S. levels this year without prompting a selloff in the Canadian dollar, analysts said.
Spreads between Canadian and U.S. bonds have also come in sharply this year, with Canadian bond yields trading below those in the U.S. as far up the curve as five years.

"I think we're already seeing a lot of the favorable outflow from a much improved current account in our bond markets over the past year," said Nesbitt Burns' Porter. "The bottom line is that bond spreads should continue to narrow, and it's supportive of the Canadian dollar as well.
I.D.E.A.'s Kalirai said Canada-U.S. spreads will likely fall to 60 basis points at the 30-year level and 35 to 40 basis points at the 10 year level by year's end.
At the close of trading Thursday, the spread at the 30-year level was 83 basis points and the spread at the 10-year level was 57 basis points.
